request: For a detector-calibration spreadsheet, what electron mass does the 2024 PDG Review of Particle Physics list? Give both printed values, in MeV/c² and in kg, including the parenthetical uncertainties.
In the 2024 PDG cosmic-ray review, what energy threshold defines ultra-high-energy cosmic rays (UHECRs)? State whether the threshold is inclusive or exclusive.
For a preliminary Mars-lander pressure-model input, what surface pressure does the NASA Mars Fact Sheet, as available on 2026-11-21, give at mean radius? What seasonal range does it state?

For a simple Jupiter thermal model, what temperatures does the NASA Jupiter Fact Sheet, as available on 2026-11-21, list at 1 bar and at 0.1 bar? Give the kelvin values and the Celsius values printed alongside them.
In the abstract of Planck 2018 Results: Cosmological Parameters, arXiv:1807.06209, what Hubble constant is inferred assuming base-ΛCDM? Include the uncertainty and unit.
NASA's Earth Fact Sheet lists an equatorial radius of 6378.137 km and a polar radius of 6356.752 km. What is the equatorial-minus-polar radius difference, in km?
ESA's Gaia factsheet lists a launch mass of 2030 kg, including 400 kg of propellant. For a mass-budget audit, what percentage of the launch mass was propellant? Round to one decimal place.

For a rough comparison of two test-chamber set points, use the NASA fact sheets' listed Earth surface pressure and Mars surface pressure at mean radius, as available on 2026-11-21. What is Earth pressure divided by Mars pressure, to one decimal place? Use the Mars mean-radius value, not its seasonal extremes.

An atmosphere-model code still uses the uncorrected Sutherland constant from U.S. Standard Atmosphere, 1976. According to NASA's errata for NTRS 19770009539, what value of S should be entered, and by how much was the document's value too small?

For a sea-level heat-transfer calculation using U.S. Standard Atmosphere, 1976, Table III prints kt = 2.5362 × 10−5 J/(m·s·K) at 0 m geometric altitude. NASA's errata says this entry is too small by a factor of 1000. What corrected kt should be used, in J/(m·s·K), and what is the same value in W/(m·K)?

A detector analyst wants to apply Eq. (34.5) of the 2024 PDG passage-of-particles review at βγ = 0.01 and claim the review's few-percent accuracy. Does the stated validity region support that use? Give the βγ region over which that accuracy is stated.

A report needs a measured neutrino-mass sum from Planck 2018. In version v4 of arXiv:1807.06209, does the result combining with BAO quote a measured value for Σmν? State exactly what constraint it gives and the confidence level the abstract assigns to upper limits.

A magnetosphere worksheet frozen on 2026-11-21 uses the symbol Rj specifically for the Jovian model radius, not a measured mean or equatorial radius. What numerical value and unit does the public planetary reference give, and how does it define Rj?

For detector-background budgeting, what illustration does the 2024 PDG passage-of-particles review give for the rarity of high-energy δ rays? Specifically, for a β ≈ 1 particle, how many collisions with Te > 10 keV occur on average along 90 cm of argon gas?

6
HIGHLIGHTS OF THE 2024 EDITION OF THE REVIEW OF PARTICLE PHYSICS
All PDG data and review articles are available online at pdg.lbl.gov.
869 new papers with 2,717 new measurements
• 320 new measurements from LHC
experiments (ATLAS, CMS and LHCb).
• Extensive Higgs boson coverage from 231
new papers and 557 measurements with
latest results on mass, couplings, decay
width and branching ratios, plus searches
for other neutral and charged Higgs bosons.
• Supersymmetry: 36 new papers with 148
measurements with major exclusions.
• Top quark: 35 new papers provide latest
results on mass, coupling, and the discovery
of four top quark production at LHC.
• W mass: CDF published a new measure-ment of the W mass. It is more precise
than the world average at the time, but the
two results disagree. See comments in
Particle Listings and our W mass review
referencing the extensive studies done by
the LHC TeV MW working group.
• c-, b-hadron physics: 161 papers and 597
measurements provide world-best data on
lifetimes, mixing, CP violation, CKM
angles, and constraints on new physics.
• Neutrino Physics: 10 new papers with
measurements on neutrino mass, mixing,
and CP-violation.
• Meson resonances: Substantial improve-ments, including new cross particle fits
involving J/ψ(1S), ψ2S) and ηc(1S),
merging of π1(1400) and π1(1600) with
non-qq¯ quantum numbers into same node,
listing of complex pole positions when
available, and inclusion of recently observed
states. Several mesons now considered
established added to Summary Tables.
• New naming scheme for the many recently
discovered mesons and baryons with c or b
quarks that are not compatible with
conventional qq¯ or qqq structures. Listed in
“Other mesons” and “Exotic baryons”
sections.
120 reviews (most are revised)
• Major revision of Higgs Physics review
summarizes latest LHC results and
constraints on new physics.
• Major revision of Cosmic rays review, now
covering all components of cosmic rays
including neutrinos (which were previously
discussed in Neutrino Telescopes in Particle
Detectors for Non-Accelerator Physics).
• Major revison of Large time-projection
chambers for rare event detection in
Particle Detectors for Non-Accelerator
Physics.
• Major revision of Top Quark review
summarizes latest LHC results and
constraints on new physics from top quark.
• Major revision of Heavy Non-qq¯ Mesons
review follows new naming scheme for
states not compatible with qq¯ or qqq
structures.
• Semiconductor detectors section of Particle
Detectors at Accelerators review includes
recent developments.
• New section on goodness-of-fit tests and
expanded discussion of statistical tests in
Statistics review.
• Updated EWK fit in Electroweak Model
and Constraints on New Physics review.
• Semileptonic B Hadron Decays,
Determination of Vcb and Vub includes
latest results and discusses long-standing
issues with inclusive and exclusive
measurements.
• Updated cross section results in the
Neutrino Cross Section Measurements
review.
• Updated τ decay parameters and
branching ratio (BR) fits, including new
treatment of BR(a1(1260) → πγ).

verdict.summary:
# Electron mass — 2024 PDG Review of Particle Physics (spreadsheet draft entry)

STATUS: draft for review by a qualified scientist before use in the detector-calibration spreadsheet. Not for publication as-is.

## 1. The printed entry (verbatim)

From the 2024 Review of Particle Physics, "Physical Constants" table (Reviews volume, file rpp2024-rev-phys-constants.pdf), and reproduced identically in the 2024 Particle Physics Booklet (db2024.pdf, p. 1):

    electron mass   m_e   0.510 998 950 00(15) MeV/c^2  =  9.109 383 7015(28)×10^-31 kg      0.30

(the trailing 0.30 is the column headed "Uncertainty (ppb)"; the table's preamble states "The 1-σ uncertainties are given in parentheses.")

Source citation, in the form PDG itself requests for a specific part of the Review:

    S. Navas et al. (Particle Data Group), Phys. Rev. D 110, 030001 (2024) — "Physical Constants" table.
    https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-phys-constants.pdf (accessed 2026-11-23; sha256 864924334c4b)

## 2. The two values, expanded

| Quantity | Printed form | Expanded (value ± 1σ) | Relative uncertainty |
|---|---|---|---|
| Electron rest mass, MeV/c² | 0.510 998 950 00(15) MeV/c² | 0.510 998 950 00 ± 0.000 000 000 15 MeV/c² | 2.94×10⁻¹⁰ = 0.29 ppb |
| Electron rest mass, kg | 9.109 383 7015(28)×10⁻³¹ kg | (9.109 383 7015 ± 0.000 000 0028)×10⁻³¹ kg, i.e. ± 2.8×10⁻⁴⁰ kg | 3.07×10⁻¹⁰ = 0.31 ppb |

PDG prints a single relative uncertainty of **0.30 ppb** for the entry; recomputing from each printed ± gives 0.29 ppb (MeV/c²) and 0.31 ppb (kg), which are the same number at PDG's two-digit rounding. Both figures are 1σ.

Notation: PDG's X(Y) means the 1σ uncertainty is Y in units of the last printed digits of X. Both numbers above are for the **rest mass**; they are not the mass–energy equivalent (0.510 998 950 00 MeV) and not a mass ratio.

## 3. Independent corroboration within the 2024 edition

The electron particle listing (rpp2024-list-electron.pdf, page 1, created 5/31/2024 10:15) gives the same quantity in three datablocks:

- Mass in u: 548.579909065 ± 0.000000016 (×10⁻⁶ u) — TIESINGA 21, RVUE, "2018 CODATA value".
- Mass in MeV: 0.51099895000 ± 0.00000000015 MeV — TIESINGA 21, RVUE, "2018 CODATA value". (Identical to the parenthetical form above.)
- The listing's preamble states: "The mass is known more precisely in u (atomic mass units) than in MeV. The conversion is: 1 u = 931.494 102 42(28) MeV/c² (2018 CODATA value, TIESINGA 21). The conversion error dominates the uncertainty of the masses given below."

So the MeV/c² uncertainty is set by the u→MeV conversion constant, not by the mass ratio measurement; this matters if the spreadsheet ever re-derives the mass from u.

## 4. Consistency check of the two printed values (no derivation required)

PDG prints the kg value directly; the spreadsheet must therefore quote it as printed, not convert. As an audit check only:

- 0.510 998 950 00 MeV × 1.602 176 634×10⁻¹³ J/MeV = 8.187 105 78×10⁻¹⁴ J (the MeV→J factor is exact in SI 2019).
- Divide by c² = 8.987 551 787 37×10¹⁶ m² s⁻² (c = 299 792 458 m s⁻¹, exact):
  8.187 105 78×10⁻¹⁴ / 8.987 551 787 37×10¹⁶ = 9.109 383 7×10⁻³¹ kg.
- Printed kg value: 9.109 383 7015(28)×10⁻³¹ kg. Agreement to the 8 significant figures carried in this hand arithmetic; residual < 1×10⁻⁸ relative is consistent with truncation in the hand division, not with a discrepancy in the source.

Uncertainty propagation through that same conversion (exact factors only) gives 9.109 383 7015×10⁻³¹ × 2.94×10⁻¹⁰ = 2.7×10⁻⁴⁰ kg, versus the printed 2.8×10⁻⁴⁰ kg. This is a last-digit difference in PDG's own CODATA derivation. **Rule for the spreadsheet: quote each printed uncertainty with its own printed value; do not replace either with the propagated one.**

## 5. What PDG does *not* print here (caveats for the reviewer)

1. **Basis is CODATA 2018, not CODATA 2022.** Footnote 'a' of the 2024 constants table reads: "Updated values reflecting the '2022 CODATA recommended values', released online in May 2024, will be incorporated in future editions of the Review." The 2024 PDG value is the TIESINGA 21 / 2018 CODATA value. If the calibration requires CODATA 2022, it must be sourced from the CODATA/NIST publication directly — no CODATA-2022 number is quoted here because none was verified in a fetched source.
2. **Sample size.** This is a single least-squares-adjusted recommended value (DOCUMENT ID TIESINGA 21, technique RVUE), not a mean of n independent measurements. The number of input measurements entering the CODATA adjustment is not stated in the cited pages; the spreadsheet should record "n not stated in source" rather than a fabricated n.
3. **Precision of the source vs. need.** The quoted relative uncertainty (≈3×10⁻¹⁰) is many orders of magnitude below any detector-calibration uncertainty; quoting 12 significant figures is for traceability, not for numerical need.
4. **Edition/format.** The same numbers appear in the Reviews volume, the Booklet, and the particle listing. Cite the Reviews "Physical Constants" table as primary (done above) and note the listing as corroboration, because the Booklet is explicitly an extract and its layout can be re-typeset between editions.

## 6. Spreadsheet-ready entry block (copy into the calibration workbook)

| Field | Entry |
|---|---|
| Quantity | Electron rest mass, m_e |
| Value (MeV/c²), printed | 0.510 998 950 00(15) MeV/c² |
| Value (MeV/c²), numeric | 0.51099895000 |
| Unc 1σ (MeV/c²), numeric | 0.00000000015 |
| Value (kg), printed | 9.109 383 7015(28)×10⁻³¹ kg |
| Value (kg), numeric | 9.1093837015E-31 |
| Unc 1σ (kg), numeric | 2.8E-40 |
| Relative uncertainty (as printed) | 0.30 ppb (1σ) |
| Value (u), corroborating | 548.579 909 065(16)×10⁻⁶ u |
| Source | S. Navas et al. (Particle Data Group), Phys. Rev. D 110, 030001 (2024), "Physical Constants" table |
| URL / access | https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-phys-constants.pdf, accessed 2026-11-23 |
| Underlying adjustment | CODATA 2018 (TIESINGA 21, RVUE) |
| n | not stated in source (single adjusted value) |
| Status | draft — pending review by qualified scientist |

If a single working number is needed for calibration arithmetic, use **m_e = 0.510 998 95 MeV/c² (relative uncertainty 3×10⁻¹⁰)** or **9.109 383 70×10⁻³¹ kg**, and keep the full printed strings above in the traceability columns.

## 7. Reviewer checklist (three items)

1. Confirm the spreadsheet is keyed to the 2024 edition (Phys. Rev. D 110, 030001 (2024)) and not to a later edition that adopts CODATA 2022.
2. Confirm the two numbers were transcribed as printed — 0.510 998 950 00(15) MeV/c² and 9.109 383 7015(28)×10⁻³¹ kg — with no rounding applied.
3. Confirm the calibration does not require a kg value re-derived from MeV/c²; if it does, the propagated uncertainty is 2.7×10⁻⁴⁰ kg, not the printed 2.8×10⁻⁴⁰ kg, and the difference should be recorded.

2f. Note that the intensity can be also defined in reference to particle energy per nucleon or
rigidity. To stress this, often the intensity is written as dJ/dE, dJ/dEn or dJ/dR.

last 20 years, the nature and identity of their sources as well as the acceleration mechanisms that
boost the particles to these extreme energies remain open questions. The understanding of CRs is
mainly derived from analyzing their energy spectrum, several observables sensitive to their primary
nature, and their arrival direction distribution. This is a challenging task mainly due to the small
flux, with less than 1 particle per km2 per year above 30EeV (see Fig. 30.1), but also because the
properties of CRs in this energy range can only be inferred indirectly from measurements of the
EAS whose description relies on extrapolations of particle physics properties at energies several
orders of magnitude above those achieved in terrestrial accelerators. Last but not least, since CRs
are charged they are deflected by the galactic and intergalactic magnetic fields and their arrival
directions at Earth point back only approximately to their actual sources.

As a neutral component of cosmic rays, γ-rays directly reach the earth from their sources, thus
allowing us to identify the origin of the photons by association with known celestial objects or
events. As shown in Figure 30.9, the source-associated contributions are revealed directly by the
bright spots whose sizes are due to the point-spread-function (PSF) of the instruments and the
intrinsic spatial extensions of the sources. It is also clearly shown that the sources are divided into
two groups: Galactic and extragalactic.

30. Cosmic Rays 237
30. Cosmic Rays
Written October 2023 by J. Alvarez-Muñiz (Santiago de Compostela U.),
Z. Cao (IHEP Beijing), U.F. Katz (Erlangen U.), P. Mertsch (TTK,
RWTH) and C. Spiering (DESY, Zeuthen).
Cosmic rays (CRs) are a non-thermal population of particles that
pervade the Universe. Their salient characteristics can be inferred from
their major observational properties: spectrum, composition and arrival
directions. For charged CRs, the energies extend from tens of MeV to
close to 1 ZeV, the flux is ∼ 104 m−2
s−1
sr−1 above 1 GeV, but the dif-ferential spectrum falls steeply with energy E, following a power-law
dependence E−γ. The most striking spectral features are the “knee” at
a few PeV where the spectral index γ changes from ∼ 2.7 to ∼ 3, the
“second knee” at ∼ 100 PeV with a change to ∼ 3.3 and the “ankle” at a
few EeV where γ changes to ∼ 2.5. The flux is largely suppressed above a
few tens of EeV. Charged CRs are composed mostly of protons, helium,
and other nuclei, as well as electrons, positrons and anti-protons. In
the detection of CRs, two classes of techniques are distinguished: direct
observations, making use of the interactions of CRs in particle physics

36.2 High-energy cosmic-ray hadron and gamma-ray detectors
36.2.1 Atmospheric fluorescence detectors
Revised March 2024 by L.R. Wiencke (Colorado School of Mines).
Cosmic-ray fluorescence detectors (FDs) use the atmosphere as a giant calorimeter to measure
isotropic scintillation light that traces the development profiles of extensive air showers. An exten-sive air shower (EAS) is produced by the interactions of ultra high-energy (E > 1017 eV) subatomic
particles in the stratosphere and upper troposphere. The amount of scintillation light generated by
an EAS is proportional to the energy deposited in the atmosphere and nearly independent of the
primary species. With energies extending beyond 1020 eV, ultra high energy cosmic rays (UHE-CRs) are the highest energy subatomic particles known to exist. In addition to particle arrival
directions, energy spectra and primary composition, the astroparticle science investigated with
FDs also includes multi-messenger studies, searches for high energy photons, neutrinos, monopoles

verdict.summary:
# UHECR energy threshold in the 2024 PDG Review of Particle Physics
## Documentary verification note — draft for review before citation or publication

No experiment was designed or run; no data were analysed. This is a source-verification memo. Every number below is either quoted verbatim from the 2024 Review of Particle Physics (RPP 2024) or is an exact unit conversion of a quoted number (conversions are exact by definition of the SI-prefixed energy units used in the field: 1 PeV ≡ 10^15 eV, 1 EeV ≡ 10^18 eV, 1 ZeV ≡ 10^21 eV).

---

## 1. Questions as posed, and how each is dispositioned

| # | Kind | Question | Disposition |
|---|------|----------|-------------|
| 1 | constraint | The threshold must come from 'the 2024 PDG cosmic-ray review' | **Blocked** — the chapter attribution cannot be verified from the retrieved text (see §7). The number reported is from Chapter 36 of the same 2024 edition. |
| 2 | value | What energy threshold defines UHECRs? | **Answered**: 10^17 eV (= 100 PeV = 0.1 EeV) |
| 3 | verdict | Inclusive or exclusive? | **Answered**: exclusive (strict inequality, E > 10^17 eV) |

---

## 2. Source identity (so a reviewer can check every quote)

**Edition.** S. Navas et al. (Particle Data Group), *Review of Particle Physics*, Phys. Rev. D **110**, 030001 (2024). '2024' therefore denotes the edition/publication year, not the year of the underlying literature: the Cosmic Rays chapter text was written October 2023 and the PDF carries the typesetting stamp *19th September, 2024 1:11pm*.

**Chapter 30, 'Cosmic Rays'** — written October 2023 by J. Alvarez-Muñiz (Santiago de Compostela U.), Z. Cao (IHEP Beijing), U.F. Katz (Erlangen U.), P. Mertsch (TTK, RWTH), C. Spiering (DESY, Zeuthen).
URL: https://pdgweb.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-cosmic-rays.pdf
Retrieved 2026-11-23T11:49:20Z; sha256 `c8f0620d58d3`; page stamp *19th September, 2024 1:11pm*.

**Chapter 36, 'Particle Detectors for Non-Accelerator Physics'**, §36.2 revised March 2024 by L.R. Wiencke (Colorado School of Mines).
URL: https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-particle-detectors-non-accel.pdf
Retrieved 2026-11-23T11:49:22Z; sha256 `92b8d56c8743`; page stamp *31st May, 2024 10:17am*.

**Also checked for a competing definition (none found):** the 2024 reviews contents page (sha256 `546364a69cbd`), the Astrophysics & Cosmology index (sha256 `79feac8c9572`), the 2024 Highlights (sha256 `6e206d3bc575`), and the Booklet front matter (sha256 `fffa63acbd33`). The Highlights note only that the Cosmic rays review received a *'Major revision … now covering all components of cosmic rays including neutrinos'* — it gives no threshold.

---

## 3. What Chapter 30 (the cosmic-ray review) actually says about the highest energies

All quotes verbatim from the PDF above; ellipses mark omitted text only.

1. Opening paragraph, p. 1: *"For charged CRs, the energies extend from tens of MeV to close to 1 ZeV, the flux is ∼10^4 m^−2 s^−1 sr^−1 above 1 GeV, but the differential spectrum falls steeply with energy E, following a power-law dependence E^−γ. The most striking spectral features are the 'knee' at a few PeV where the spectral index γ changes from ∼2.7 to ∼3, the 'second knee' at ∼100 PeV with a change to ∼3.3 and the 'ankle' at a few EeV where γ changes to ∼2.5. The flux is largely suppressed above a few tens of EeV."*
2. Introduction, p. 1–2: *"…the small flux, with less than 1 particle per km^2 per year above 30EeV (see Fig. 30.1)…"*
3. §30.3.2 (gamma rays), p. 19–20: *"…from the cascade of very-high-energy gamma rays and UHECRs are not ruled out as a fraction of the extragalactic diffuse emission."*

**Reading.** In the retrieved text the acronym 'UHECR' is *used* (item 3) but never *defined* by a numeric threshold. Items 1 and 2 are descriptions of the measured spectrum and flux (spectral features; a flux reference point), not definitions of a particle-energy class. Item 1's 'close to 1 ZeV' (= 10^21 eV) is an upper reach of the observed spectrum, not a lower threshold.

**Coverage caveat (this is the crux of the blocked ask).** Chapter 30 runs to roughly 30 PDF pages (running heads '30. Cosmic Rays' appear through p. 20 and beyond in the retrieved material). The grounding supplies ~5 paragraphs of it. Absence of a definitional sentence in those paragraphs is **not** evidence of absence in the chapter.

---

## 4. The explicit numeric statement in RPP 2024 (Chapter 36)

Verbatim, §36.2.1 'Atmospheric fluorescence detectors', p. 2 of the chapter PDF:

> *"An extensive air shower (EAS) is produced by the interactions of ultra high-energy (E > 10^17 eV) subatomic particles in the stratosphere and upper troposphere."*

> *"With energies extending beyond 10^20 eV, ultra high energy cosmic rays (UHECRs) are the highest energy subatomic particles known to exist."*

This is the **only definitional construction of the form 'ultra high-energy (E > X)'** present anywhere in the retrieved 2024 RPP text. The second sentence attaches an energy to the term UHECR itself, but in a descriptive form ('with energies extending beyond 10^20 eV'), describing the reach of the population rather than setting a lower boundary of the class.

---

## 5. Answer

**Ask 2 — threshold: 10^17 eV = 100 PeV = 0.1 EeV.**
- Quantity: energy **per particle** (the standard cosmic-ray convention; the source's own definition of intensity allows per-nucleon and per-rigidity variants — *"the intensity can be also defined in reference to particle energy per nucleon or rigidity … often the intensity is written as dJ/dE, dJ/dEn or dJ/dR"* — but the Chapter 36 threshold is stated for the particle, not per nucleon).
- Kinetic vs total energy: the source does not distinguish. The distinction is numerically irrelevant here: a nucleon rest mass is 0.938 GeV = 9.38 × 10^8 eV, i.e. 9.4 × 10^−9 of 10^17 eV, far below the one-decade precision at which the threshold is stated.
- **Uncertainty: none quoted.** The source gives no ± and no confidence interval; it is an order-of-magnitude convention, so the meaningful precision is one decade (10^17 eV, not 1.0 × 10^17 eV). **Sample size: not applicable** — no measurement underlies the number.

**Ask 3 — verdict: EXCLUSIVE.** The source writes a strict inequality, *E > 10^17 eV* — energies strictly greater than 10^17 eV; 10^17 eV exactly is not included. The second statement ('extending beyond 10^20 eV') is likewise exclusive.

**Provenance statement that must travel with the number.** The threshold is printed in Chapter 36 of RPP 2024, *not* in Chapter 30 (the Cosmic Rays review) as retrieved. If the question is read as demanding a threshold printed inside the Cosmic Rays chapter, the retrieved grounding does not establish one (§7 says how to close that gap in one pass over the PDF).

---

## 6. Inventory of every energy appearing in the retrieved text (internal-consistency guard)

| Value (as printed) | In eV | Where | Inclusive/exclusive as worded | Role |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| E > 10^17 eV | 1 × 10^17 (= 100 PeV = 0.1 EeV) | §36.2.1 | **exclusive** ('>') | **The threshold reported here** |
| beyond 10^20 eV | 1 × 10^20 (= 100 EeV = 0.1 ZeV) | §36.2.1 | exclusive ('beyond') | Descriptive reach of UHECRs, not a lower boundary |
| above 30EeV | 3 × 10^19 | §30 introduction | exclusive ('above') | Flux reference (<1 particle km^−2 yr^−1) |
| above a few tens of EeV | ~10^19–10^20 | §30 p. 1 | exclusive, approximate | Spectral suppression |
| close to 1 ZeV | ~1 × 10^21 | §30 p. 1 | approximate upper end | Top of observed range |
| above 1 GeV | 1 × 10^9 | §30 p. 1 | exclusive | Flux normalization |
| a few PeV / ~100 PeV / a few EeV | ~10^15 / 10^17 / ~10^18 | §30 p. 1 | approximate | Knee / second knee / ankle |
| 2 PeV, 0.1 PeV, 0.1 GeV, 30 GeV–100 TeV, few hundred GeV | 2×10^15, 1×10^14, 1×10^8, 3×10^10–1×10^14, ~10^11 | §30 §30.3, §36 §36.2 | various | Gamma-ray astronomy / detector ranges — not UHECR thresholds |

**Two consistency traps, flagged explicitly so no reader is misled:**

1. **100 PeV is both the §30 'second knee' and the §36 UHE threshold.** They are numerically identical (10^17 eV) but conceptually unrelated — a spectral feature versus a detector-regime boundary. They must not be merged into one claim.
2. **The field's common convention is ~1 EeV = 10^18 eV, one decade above the value reported here.** That convention is *not* what the retrieved PDG text states, and it is *not* the answer given. It sits near the §30 'ankle' ('a few EeV'), and a reviewer who expects 10^18 eV should be shown this table rather than silently accommodated.

---

## 7. What a reviewer must do to close the provenance gap (ask 1)

One pass over the full Chapter 30 PDF (≈30 pp.):

1. Search the terms `UHECR`, `ultra-high-energy`, `ultra high energy`, `EeV`, `ZeV`, `10^18`, `10^19`.
2. Check the sections the retrieved excerpts do not cover: §30.2.2 (indirect observations / EAS), the highest-energy spectrum discussion around Fig. 30.7, and the composition/anisotropy sections (§30.3–30.4 region).
3. If Chapter 30 prints its own threshold — plausibly *E > 10^18 eV* (1 EeV) or *E > 10^19 eV* — that value **supersedes** the Chapter 36 number for the literal question, and asks 2 and 3 must be re-issued. Inclusivity is then read off the wording: 'above', 'in excess of', 'beyond', '>' ⇒ exclusive; 'at or above', 'in excess of or equal to', '≥' ⇒ inclusive.
4. Also confirm no glossary defines UHECRs in the Booklet (sha256 `fffa63acbd33`) — none was found in the retrieved front matter.

---

## 8. Citation-ready sentences (choose according to how strictly the question is read)

**(a) Answer as issued (recommended, with provenance attached):**
> The 2024 Review of Particle Physics sets the ultra-high-energy threshold at E > 10^17 eV (100 PeV, 0.1 EeV), exclusive; the statement appears in Chapter 36, 'Particle Detectors for Non-Accelerator Physics' (§36.2.1, revised March 2024), which also describes UHECRs as having energies 'extending beyond 10^20 eV' (S. Navas et al., Particle Data Group, Phys. Rev. D 110, 030001 (2024)).

**(b) Strict-to-chapter wording, if a reviewer requires the threshold to come from the Cosmic Rays review itself:**
> The 2024 PDG Cosmic Rays review (Chapter 30) describes the spectrum as 'largely suppressed above a few tens of EeV' with energies extending 'close to 1 ZeV', but does not, in the text verified here, print a single numeric definition of the UHECR threshold; the only definitional statement in the 2024 edition is E > 10^17 eV in Chapter 36.

---

*Prepared as a documentary verification draft. It reports what the cited 2024 PDG text says, not an independent determination of where UHECRs 'should' begin; the choice of a decade boundary is a community convention, and the source quotes no uncertainty for it.*

which the planet is closest to the Sun, the perihelion, and a point furthest from the Sun, the aphelion.
The average distance from the Sun is midway between these two values.  The average distance from the Earth
to the Sun is defined as 1 Astronomical Unit (AU), so the ratio table gives this distance in AU.

Perihelion, Aphelion (106 km or 106 miles) - The closest and furthest points

* For the Moon, the closest and furthest points to Earth are given, known as the "Perigee" and "Apogee"
respectively.
Orbital Period (days)  -  This is the time in Earth days for a planet to orbit the Sun from one
vernal equinox to the next.  Also known as the tropical orbit period, this is equal to a year on Earth.
* For the Moon, the sidereal orbit period, the time to orbit once relative to the fixed background
stars, is given.  The time from full Moon to full Moon, or synodic period, is 29.53 days.
For Pluto, the tropical orbit period is not well known, the sidereal orbit period is used.

verdict.summary:
DRAFT EXTRACTION FOR REVIEW — Mars surface pressure input, NASA/NSSDCA Mars Fact Sheet (not for publication or model use until a qualified scientist signs off)

1. SOURCE AND VERSION CONTROL (satisfies ask 2)
- Document: 'Mars Fact Sheet', NASA Goddard Space Flight Center, NSSDCA; Author/Curator Dr. David R. Williams; NASA Official Thomas Morgan.
- URL retrieved: https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary//factsheet/marsfact.html
- Retrieval timestamp: 2026-11-23T11:53:22Z; content sha256 366b0ce9b69c (prefix as recorded).
- Page's own version stamp: 'Last Updated: 19 May 2025, DRW'.
- Availability on 2026-11-21: the page's last-modified stamp (19 May 2025) predates the requested date, and the same stamp was still present on the page fetched 2026-11-23 (two days after the requested date). The page text in force on 2026-11-21 is therefore the text quoted below. Residual caveat, stated for the reviewer: no archived snapshot with a capture date on or before 2026-11-21 was retrieved, so this rests on the last-updated stamp plus the unchanged 2026-11-23 fetch, not on a dated archive copy. Supporting context: the NSSDCA fact-sheet index (https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/, fetched 2026-11-23T11:53:22Z, sha256 4eec48c66526) carries 'Last Updated: 13 November 2026, SAM', i.e. the index was touched before 2026-11-21 while the Mars page itself was not re-stamped.
- Publisher's own disclaimer on the notes page (https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary//factsheet/fact_notes.html, fetched 2026-11-23T11:53:22Z, sha256 549150c04a2f): 'there is no single set of agreed upon values. They are based on ongoing research and as such are under study and subject to change at any time.'

2. VERBATIM SOURCE TEXT (Martian Atmosphere block, marsfact.html)
"Surface pressure:  6.36 mb at mean radius (variable from 4.0 to 8.7 mb depending on season)"
"[6.9 mb to 9 mb (Viking 1 Lander site)]"
Same block, for context: "Surface density: ~0.016 +/- 0.006 kg/m3"; "Scale height:  11.0 km".

3. ASK 1 — SURFACE PRESSURE AT MEAN RADIUS
- Value as printed: 6.36 mb.
- Units as printed: mb (millibar). Per the fact-sheet notes, 'mb = 10^-3 bar' and '1 bar = 10^5 Pascal (Pa)'; therefore 1 mb = 100 Pa and
  6.36 mb = 636 Pa = 6.36 hPa = 0.00636 bar.
- Significant figures: three (6.36). Printed precision is 0.01 mb = 1 Pa.
- 'At mean radius' is printed on the same line as the value, so no datum-elevation inference is required. The same page defines the radius it uses under Bulk parameters: 'Volumetric mean radius (km) 3389.5', and the notes page defines that term as 'Radius of a sphere with the same volume as the body'. Mean radius for this extraction = 3389.5 km (volumetric mean).
- Uncertainty: none stated by the fact sheet for surface pressure. (The sheet does attach an uncertainty to surface density, '~0.016 +/- 0.006 kg/m3', which shows that omission for pressure is deliberate, not a transcription loss.) No uncertainty is invented here.
- Sample size / averaging basis: not stated. The fact sheet gives no number of stations, no averaging interval, and no reference year for the pressure figure. Reported as 'none stated'.

4. ASK 4 — SEASONAL RANGE STATED
- As printed: 'variable from 4.0 to 8.7 mb depending on season'.
- That is, seasonal envelope 4.0 mb to 8.7 mb = 400 Pa to 870 Pa = 0.00400 bar to 0.00870 bar.
- Significant figures as printed: two (4.0; 8.7).
- Width and asymmetry: full width 4.7 mb (470 Pa); departures from the stated 6.36 mb mean are +2.34 mb (234 Pa) high and -2.36 mb (236 Pa) low. Ratio max/min = 8.7/4.0 = 2.175.
- Internal consistency check: midpoint of the stated envelope = (4.0 + 8.7)/2 = 6.35 mb, versus the stated mean 6.36 mb; difference 0.01 mb = 1 Pa = 0.16%, i.e. one unit in the last printed place. The envelope is therefore consistent with the mean to printed precision, but it is not exactly symmetric, and no symmetry should be assumed downstream.
- Quantity the range refers to: it is attached to the mean-radius global value on the same line ('at mean radius ... variable from 4.0 to 8.7 mb depending on season'), so it is a global/seasonal (CO2-cycle) envelope about the global annual value — not a diurnal range and not a single-station range. The page gives the diurnal range separately and labels it by site ('Diurnal temperature range: 184 K to 242 K ... (Viking 1 Lander site)'), which is the pattern it uses when a value is site-specific.
- Time span / season convention: not stated (no Martian-season labels, no year range, no spacecraft or lander attribution for the 4.0-8.7 mb envelope). Reported as 'none stated'.
- Do NOT confuse with the bracketed line '6.9 mb to 9 mb (Viking 1 Lander site)'. That is a separate site-specific pressure range, is not labelled seasonal, and is not the seasonal range of the mean-radius value. Quoting 6.9-9 mb as the answer to ask 4 would be a misquotation.

5. TRAP TO FLAG FOR THE MODELLER
- The summary 'Planetary Fact Sheet - Metric' table (index page above) lists Mars 'Surface Pressure (bars) 0.01'. That is a rounding of 6.36 mb (0.00636 bar) up to 0.01 bar = 10 mb = 1000 Pa, about 57% above the detailed sheet's mean-radius value. Use 6.36 mb (636 Pa) and the 4.0-8.7 mb envelope from the Mars Fact Sheet; do not take 0.01 bar from the summary table as the model input.
- 6.36 mb is a global abstraction at the 3389.5 km volumetric mean radius. It is not the pressure at any landing site: the same page's own Viking 1 Lander site entry is 6.9-9 mb, which brackets the global mean, and real site pressures will differ further with elevation and season. A lander pressure model should carry the global mean only as a first-order reference and must not treat it as a site boundary condition.

6. TRANSCRIPTION RULE APPLIED
Values are transcribed exactly as printed, in the fact sheet's own units (mb), with no re-derivation; Pa/hPa/bar equivalents above are given only as conversions of the printed numbers using the notes page's definitions (1 mb = 100 Pa), and are marked as conversions. No uncertainty, sample size, season label, or provenance year has been supplied from outside the cited pages.

verdict.summary:
# NASA Jupiter Fact Sheet: temperatures at 1 bar and 0.1 bar

Draft for review by a qualified scientist. All values below are transcribed as printed on the source page; derived quantities are labelled as derived and are not part of the two answers.

## 1. Source identification and provenance

Primary source (the 'NASA Jupiter Fact Sheet'):

- Title: Jupiter Fact Sheet
- Publisher: NASA NSSDCA (National Space Science Data Coordinated Archive), NASA Goddard Space Flight Center. Page credits 'Author/Curator: Dr. David R. Williams, dave.williams@nasa.gov, NSSDCA, Mail Code 690.1, NASA Goddard Space Flight Center'.
- URL as retrieved: https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary//factsheet/jupiterfact.html (the doubled slash after /planetary/ is the link form used by NSSDCA's own index; the single-slash form resolves to the same document).
- Retrieval: harness fetch, 2026-11-23T11:57:06Z; document digest sha256 beginning 9ac7835ae538.
- Version evidence relative to the requested access date, 2026-11-21: the NSSDCA fact-sheet index (https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary//factsheet/index.html, same fetch) prints 'Last Updated: 13 November 2026, SAM', and the planetary fact-sheet landing page (https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/planetfact.html, same fetch) prints 'Last Updated: September 08, 2026'. Both revision stamps precede 2026-11-21, so the copy fetched two days after the target date carries no revision that post-dates it.
- Stated caveat: no Internet Archive / Wayback capture dated 2026-11-21 was retrieved in this session. The identity of the 2026-11-21 version is therefore inferred from the pre-target revision stamps, not directly witnessed by a dated snapshot. This is a provenance caveat, not a reason to withhold the values: the document itself was retrieved, and its revision metadata predates the requested date.

## 2. The relevant section, verbatim

Under the heading 'Jovian Atmosphere', the page prints, in this order:

    Surface Pressure: >>1000 bars
    Temperature at 1 bar: 165 K (-108 C)
    Temperature at 0.1 bar: 112 K (-161 C)
    Density at 1 bar: 0.16 kg/m3
    Wind speeds
    Up to 150 m/s (<30 degrees latitude)
    Up to  40 m/s (>30 degrees latitude)
    Scale height: 27 km
    Mean molecular weight: 2.22

## 3. Answers, as printed (not recomputed)

| Pressure level | Temperature (K), as printed | Temperature (C), as printed | Exact conversion of the printed kelvin value |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 bar | 165 | -108 | -108.15 |
| 0.1 bar | 112 | -161 | -161.15 |

The page prints the units as 'K' and as 'C' (degrees Celsius) and prints the Celsius value in parentheses directly alongside the kelvin value. Both printed values are integers; no uncertainty, error bar or significant-figure statement accompanies either temperature.

## 4. Verification of the printed conversions

165 - 273.15 = -108.15, which rounds to the printed -108. 112 - 273.15 = -161.15, which rounds to the printed -161. Both printed Celsius values are therefore the correctly rounded (to the nearest 1 degree C) conversions of the printed kelvin values, with a residual of 0.15 degrees C in each case, i.e. within the +/-0.5 degree C quantisation of a 1-degree printed value. The two printed pairs are mutually consistent and no transcription or conversion error is detectable. The printed values are reported unchanged; no recomputation or re-rounding is applied.

## 5. Units, precision, uncertainty and sample size

- K: SI base unit of thermodynamic temperature. Degrees C = K - 273.15 (exact).
- bar: per the same site's Notes on the Fact Sheets (https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/fact_notes.html), 1 bar = 10^5 Pa = 10^5 kg m^-1 s^-2.
- The page's own line 'Surface Pressure: >>1000 bars' means both quoted levels are pressure levels inside the atmosphere, well above any notional surface; they are not surface temperatures.
- Printed resolution: +/-0.5 K and +/-0.5 degrees C (integer last digit). The fact sheet prints no measurement or model uncertainty for these two temperatures.
- Sample size: n = 2 printed values from 1 document from 1 retrieval. This is a documentary lookup, not a statistical sample; there is no replicate count and no averaging is possible or appropriate.

## 6. Cross-checks: why these two values and not neighbouring ones

- 'Black-body temperature (K) 109.9' (Bulk parameters block, same Jupiter page) is Jupiter's effective/black-body temperature. It is not the 0.1-bar atmospheric temperature (112 K) and must not be substituted for it. The two are numerically close but physically distinct quantities.
- The Planetary Fact Sheet - Metric table (https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary//factsheet/index.html) lists Jupiter 'Mean Temperature (C) -110'. That is a single whole-planet mean with no pressure level attached; it is not the 1-bar value (-108 C) and must not be substituted.
- science.nasa.gov 'Jupiter Facts' (https://science.nasa.gov/jupiter/jupiter-facts/, page last updated 2026-10-15) was retrieved and contains no 1-bar/0.1-bar temperature pair; it is not the source for this answer.
- The Notes on the Fact Sheets define 'Average temperature' as the mean over the entire surface in kelvin and define the bar, but do not separately define a pressure-level temperature. The 1 bar / 0.1 bar convention on the Jupiter page is therefore used exactly as printed, with no site-supplied definition attached to it.

## 7. Use in a simple thermal model (derived; not printed on the page)

The two printed levels bracket a 53 K drop over one decade of pressure: delta-T = 165 - 112 = 53 K, with +/-1 K propagated from the +/-0.5 K quantisation of each printed value.

Height separation, from the isothermal hydrostatic relation delta-z = H ln(p1/p2) = H ln 10 = 2.302585 H:

- Using the page's printed scale height H = 27 km: delta-z = 62.2 km (+/-1.2 km, from a +/-0.5 km reading of the printed H), giving a mean lapse rate of 53 / 62.2 = 0.85 K/km.
- Using a scale height self-consistent with the printed temperatures, H = R T / (mu g), with R = 8.314 J mol^-1 K^-1, mu = 2.22 x 10^-3 kg/mol and g = 25.92 m s^-2 (the last two both printed on the same page, g as 'Gravity (mean, 1 bar) 25.92 m/s2'), evaluated at the mean of the two levels T = 138.5 K: H = 20.0 km, delta-z = 46.1 km, giving a mean lapse rate of 1.15 K/km.

A simple model of the 1-to-0.1 bar layer should therefore be anchored on the printed endpoints (165 K at 1 bar, 112 K at 0.1 bar) and, if an intermediate profile is needed, use a linear-in-ln(p) interpolation corresponding to a mean lapse rate of roughly 0.85-1.15 K/km. The endpoints are the documented constraint; the profile between them is model-dependent.

Consistency warning worth flagging to the modeller: the printed scale height of 27 km implies T = H mu g / R = 27000 x 0.0575424 / 8.314 = 186.9 K, i.e. about 187 K, which is 22 K warmer than the printed 1-bar temperature of 165 K. The printed scale height is therefore not self-consistent with the printed 1-bar temperature under the printed mean molecular weight and gravity, and the two should not be combined without stating which convention is used. This is why the lapse rate is quoted as a range (0.85 K/km under the 27 km convention, 1.15 K/km under the self-consistent convention) rather than as a single number.

Uncertainty on the derived lapse rate: about +/-0.02 K/km from the printed quantisation alone; the systematic spread between the two scale-height conventions (0.85 versus 1.15 K/km) dominates and should be quoted instead.

## 8. What would change this answer

The answer is a transcription of two printed lines. It would change only if a snapshot of the same URL demonstrably dated on or before 2026-11-21 showed different printed values. The pre-target 'Last Updated' stamps on the two NSSDCA pages that link to this document (13 November 2026 and 08 September 2026) argue against any such intervening revision, and no conflicting snapshot was found in this session.

spatially-flat 6-parameter ΛCDM cosmology having a power-law spectrum of adiabatic scalar perturbations (denoted “base ΛCDM” in this paper),
from polarization, temperature, and lensing, separately and in combination. A combined analysis gives dark matter density Ωch
2 = 0.120 ± 0.001,
baryon density Ωbh
2 = 0.0224 ± 0.0001, scalar spectral index ns = 0.965 ± 0.004, and optical depth τ = 0.054 ± 0.007 (in this abstract we quote
68 % confidence regions on measured parameters and 95 % on upper limits). The angular acoustic scale is measured to 0.03 % precision, with
100θ∗ = 1.0411±0.0003. These results are only weakly dependent on the cosmological model and remain stable, with somewhat increased errors,
in many commonly considered extensions. Assuming the base-ΛCDM cosmology, the inferred (model-dependent) late-Universe parameters are:
Hubble constant H0 = (67.4±0.5) km s−1Mpc−1
; matter density parameter Ωm = 0.315±0.007; and matter fluctuation amplitude σ8 = 0.811±0.006.

quotes.whole:
As a consequence, the current ACTPol and SPTpol polariza-tion constraints on the parameters of the base-ΛCDM cosmology
are much weaker than those derived from Planck. The ACTPol
results (Louis et al. 2017) are consistent with the Planck base-ΛCDM parameters and showed a small improvement in con-straints on extensions to the base cosmology that affect the
damping tail. Similar results were found by SPTpol, though
Henning et al. (2018) noted a >∼ 2σ tension with the base-ΛCDM model and found a trend for the parameters of the base-ΛCDM model to drift away from the Planck solution as the
SPTpol likelihood is extended to higher multipoles. To assess
these results we have performed some tests of the consistency of
the latest Planck results and the SPTpol spectra.
As a reference model for SPTpol we adopt the base-ΛCDM
parameters for the combined T E + EE fit to the SPTpol data
from table 5 of Henning et al. (2018). It is worth noting that the
best-fit SPTpol cosmology is strongly excluded by the Planck

verdict.summary:
SOURCE AND PROVENANCE
Paper: Planck Collaboration VI (N. Aghanim et al. 2020), 'Planck 2018 results. VI. Cosmological parameters', A&A 641, A6; DOI 10.1051/0004-6361/201833910; arXiv:1807.06209 [astro-ph.CO], version v4 (last revised 9 Aug 2021). Abstract text as retrieved from https://arxiv.org/pdf/1807.06209.pdf on 2026-11-23T12:00:20Z (sha256 8e172730faf0). The value below is a transcription from that abstract only; no re-analysis, no re-fitting, no chain recomputation was performed or is needed.

VERBATIM QUOTE (the operative sentence of the abstract)
'Assuming the base-ΛCDM cosmology, the inferred (model-dependent) late-Universe parameters are: Hubble constant H0 = (67.4±0.5) km s−1Mpc−1; matter density parameter Ωm = 0.315±0.007; and matter fluctuation amplitude σ8 = 0.811±0.006.'

ANSWER
H0 = (67.4 ± 0.5) km s^-1 Mpc^-1 (equivalently 67.4 ± 0.5 km/s/Mpc).
- Central value: 67.4
- Uncertainty: ±0.5, a 68% confidence (credible) interval half-width. The abstract states its own convention: 'in this abstract we quote 68 % confidence regions on measured parameters and 95 % on upper limits.' The abstract prints a symmetric ±0.5, so the interval is 66.9 to 67.9 km s^-1 Mpc^-1. Relative uncertainty = 0.5/67.4 = 0.74%.
- Unit: km s^-1 Mpc^-1 (kilometres per second per megaparsec), exactly as printed in the abstract.

MODEL CONTEXT (from the same abstract, required for correct attribution)
The abstract defines the model it fits as a 'spatially-flat 6-parameter ΛCDM cosmology having a power-law spectrum of adiabatic scalar perturbations (denoted "base ΛCDM" in this paper)', constrained 'from polarization, temperature, and lensing, separately and in combination.' The abstract's phrase for the number it quotes is 'a combined analysis'. Two honest caveats for the reviewer: (i) H0 is a derived, model-dependent parameter of that fit, not a direct distance-ladder measurement, and the abstract itself labels it '(model-dependent)'; (ii) the abstract does not print the likelihood-combination tag for the quoted combined analysis. The paper's baseline tag for that combination is TT,TE,EE+lowE+lensing, but that identification comes from the body of the paper, not from the abstract sentence quoted here; it is context, not part of the extracted value. The value should not be conflated with H0 from extended models, from BAO+Planck combinations, or with late-Universe (distance-ladder) determinations; none of those are the quantity asked for.

DERIVED CONVERSIONS (computed here for convenience only; NOT in the abstract; constants: 1 Mpc = 3.0856775814913673e19 km, 1 Julian yr = 3.15576e7 s)
- H0 = 67.4/3.0856775814913673e19 s^-1 = 2.184e-18 s^-1, i.e. (2.184 ± 0.016)e-18 s^-1 (0.74% propagated in quadrature from the single quoted uncertainty).
- H0 = (6.893 ± 0.051)e-11 yr^-1.
- Hubble time 1/H0 = 4.578e17 s = 14.51 ± 0.11 Gyr.
These derived figures inherit the model dependence and the 68% confidence convention of the source value and should be quoted only with that caveat.

TRANSCRIPTION CHECKS PERFORMED
1. Digits and sign read directly from the PDF abstract string 'H0 = (67.4±0.5) km s−1Mpc−1' — no rounding, no unit conversion applied to the reported value.
2. Uncertainty convention confirmed against the abstract's own stated convention (68% for measured parameters).
3. Confidence interval arithmetic: 67.4 − 0.5 = 66.9; 67.4 + 0.5 = 67.9 km s^-1 Mpc^-1.
4. Relative error 0.5/67.4 = 0.742%, used consistently in all derived conversions above.
5. Version pinned (v4) with retrieval hash so the quoted sentence can be re-verified; if a later arXiv version or the A&A erratum-level text changed this sentence, this extraction is superseded and must be re-read from the source rather than patched.

STATUS
This is a draft extraction for a qualified scientist to check against the published PDF before use or citation. It answers all three asks with no blocked items; the only judgement call a reviewer may wish to confirm is that the abstract's 'combined analysis' value is the intended baseline (it is the only H0 the abstract quotes for base-ΛCDM).

verdict.summary: Simple reversible arithmetic comparison of two published Earth radius values.

asks.quote: What is the equatorial-minus-polar radius difference, in km?

verdict.summary:
Deliverable: equatorial-minus-polar radius difference for Earth

Result
Δr = r_eq − r_pol = 6378.137 km − 6356.752 km = 21.385 km.

The equatorial radius is larger than the polar radius by 21.385 km. Sign convention: positive means equatorial minus polar.

Calculation table
| Quantity | Value | Unit | Source / derivation |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Equatorial radius, r_eq | 6378.137 | km | NASA Earth Fact Sheet value as supplied in the request |
| Polar radius, r_pol | 6356.752 | km | NASA Earth Fact Sheet value as supplied in the request |
| Difference, Δr = r_eq − r_pol | 21.385 | km | Direct subtraction; reported to 0.001 km to match input precision |
| Relative difference, 100 × Δr / r_eq | 0.3353 | % | 100 × 21.385 / 6378.137 = 0.335286%, rounded to 0.3353% |

Units and rounding
Both radii are already in kilometers, so no unit conversion is required. The inputs are stated to three decimal places (0.001 km), and the difference is reported to the same precision: 21.385 km. The arithmetic is exact at the stated precision.

Uncertainty
NASA's Earth Fact Sheet values as supplied do not state uncertainties for these radii. If the two published numbers are treated as exact reference constants, the subtraction has no measurement uncertainty. If they are treated as values rounded to the nearest 0.001 km, then each has a half-unit rounding interval of ±0.0005 km, and the conservative worst-case bound on the difference is ±0.001 km, i.e. an interval of 21.384 km to 21.386 km. Under an independent-uniform rounding model, the standard uncertainty of the difference is sqrt(2) × 0.0005 / sqrt(3) = 0.000408 km, reported as ±0.0004 km (k = 1). This uncertainty statement does not change the central value.

Sample size and statistics
Sample size is n = 1 published reference value for each radius. These are not sample statistics, so no standard error, confidence interval, hypothesis test, or p-value is computed.

Citation format
NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive (NSSDCA), Earth Fact Sheet, NASA, https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/earthfact.html (retrieval date to be inserted by the citing author). Values used: equatorial radius 6378.137 km; polar radius 6356.752 km. The arithmetic above uses the values exactly as supplied in the request; a citing author should verify the fact sheet and insert the access date before publication.

Answer to the ask
21.385 km.
Low-risk, reversible data-analysis calculation for a mass-budget audit.

asks.quote: what percentage of the launch mass was propellant?
Round to one decimal place.

verdict.summary:
# Propellant share of Gaia launch mass — mass-budget audit calculation (draft for qualified-scientist review)

## 1. Answer
**Propellant was 19.7 % of launch mass** (1 decimal place).

400 kg ÷ 2030 kg × 100 = 19.704433… % → **19.7 %**

## 2. Inputs, source and sample size

| Symbol | Quantity | Value | Unit | Source | Reported precision |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| M_launch | Gaia launch mass, *including* propellant | 2030 | kg | ESA Gaia factsheet, as quoted in the audit request | no decimals given; treated as rounded to nearest 10 kg (§5) |
| M_prop | Propellant mass at launch | 400 | kg | ESA Gaia factsheet, as quoted in the audit request | no decimals given; treated as rounded to nearest 10 kg (§5) |

**Sample size:** n = 1 spacecraft (Gaia); 2 reported scalar masses; no replicate measurements.

**Source-record caveat (must be closed before sign-off):** the factsheet edition, document URL and access date are *not* recorded here, because I have no access to the document and will not invent a version identifier. The reviewer must insert edition/URL/access date into the audit record. This does not affect the arithmetic, which uses only the two figures quoted in the request.

**Stated assumption A1 (taken from the request's own wording):** "launch mass of 2030 kg, including 400 kg of propellant" is read as M_prop ⊂ M_launch, i.e. 2030 kg is the wet/total launch mass and the propellant is a subset of it. Under A1 the denominator is 2030 kg. §6 flag F1 gives the alternative branch in case the reviewer finds the factsheet means dry mass.

## 3. Method and arithmetic (fully reproducible)

p (%) = 100 × M_prop / M_launch

p = 100 × 400 / 2030
  = 100 × 0.1970443349753695
  = **19.70443349753695 %**

**Rounding:** half-up to one decimal place. The digit string is 19.7|044…; the deciding digit is 0, so the result is 19.7. No tie occurs, so the choice of rounding convention (half-up vs half-even) cannot change the answer.

**Reported value:** 19.7 % (equivalently mass fraction 0.197 to 3 significant figures).

**Reproduction in one line each:**
- Spreadsheet: `=ROUND(100*400/2030,1)` → 19.7
- Python 3: `round(100*400/2030, 1)` → 19.7
- R: `round(100*400/2030, 1)` → 19.7

## 4. Cross-checks (all pass)

| ID | Check | Computation | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| C1 | Complement closes to 100 % | 2030 − 400 = 1630 kg; 1630/2030 × 100 = 80.295566… → 80.3 %; 19.7 + 80.3 = 100.0 (unrounded 19.7044 + 80.2956 = 100.0000) | ✓ |
| C2 | Percentage within bounds | 0 ≤ 19.7 ≤ 100 | ✓ |
| C3 | Ordering consistent | M_prop (400 kg) < M_dry (1630 kg) and 19.7 % < 50 % | ✓ |
| C4 | Back-calculation to input | 0.197 × 2030 = 399.9 kg vs 400 kg (0.02 % closure) | ✓ |

## 5. Uncertainty — what it is and what it is not

There is **no statistical uncertainty**: n = 1 spacecraft, and the quantity is a deterministic ratio of two reported scalars. No replicate exists, so no standard error, standard deviation or confidence interval is defined, and none is quoted. The only uncertainty is **source rounding (significant figures)** of the two quoted masses.

**Sensitivity S1 — masses rounded to the nearest 10 kg (working assumption):** M_prop ∈ [395, 405] kg, M_launch ∈ [2025, 2035] kg.
- lower bound: 395 / 2035 × 100 = 19.4103 % → **19.4 %**
- upper bound: 405 / 2025 × 100 = 20.0000 % → **20.0 %**
- band **19.4 – 20.0 %** (width 0.6 percentage points; half-width ≈ 0.3 pp).
- The reported 19.7 % lies inside this band (consistency ✓). Under this worst case the one-decimal figure could be anywhere in 19.4–20.0, so the audit record should read **19.7 % (source-rounding band 19.4–20.0 %)**.

**Sensitivity S2 — masses rounded to the nearest 1 kg:**
- lower: 399.5 / 2030.5 × 100 = 19.6750 %
- upper: 400.5 / 2029.5 × 100 = 19.7339 %
- both round to **19.7 %** → the one-decimal answer is *stable* against ±0.5 kg source rounding ✓.

**Recommendation:** carry 19.7 % as the audit figure; if the audit needs a defensible tolerance, use ±0.3 pp from S1 and replace it with the factsheet's own stated precision if one is published.

## 6. Audit flags for the reviewing scientist

- **F1 — definitional (does not change the arithmetic, must be confirmed at sign-off).** Confirm that the factsheet's 2030 kg is *wet* launch mass. If 2030 kg is dry mass and the 400 kg is additional, launch mass = 2030 + 400 = 2430 kg and p = 400/2430 × 100 = 16.4609 % → **16.5 %**, i.e. **3.2 pp lower** than the reported figure. The reported answer follows the request's wording; this branch is stated so a mis-transcription can be caught.
- **F2 — source precision.** Neither figure carries decimals. If the factsheet presents 2030 kg and 400 kg as exact design values, S1 overstates the uncertainty and 19.7 % may be treated as exact to 3 s.f. (0.197).
- **F3 — scope.** The remaining 1630 kg is not decomposed by subsystem here; that breakdown is outside this request.
- **F4 — interpretation.** The figure is a mass ratio only; no propulsion-performance (Δv, Isp) inference is drawn from it.

## 7. Related ratios for the auditor's context (not the requested answer)

| Ratio | Expression | Value | Unit |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Propellant / launch mass (REQUESTED)** | 400 / 2030 | **19.7** | % |
| Non-propellant / launch mass | 1630 / 2030 | 80.3 | % |
| Propellant / non-propellant (dry) mass | 400 / 1630 | 24.5 | % |
| Propellant / launch mass under F1 (if 2030 kg were dry) | 400 / 2430 | 16.5 | % |

(400/1630 × 100 = 24.5399 % → 24.5 %.)

## 8. Figure

**Figure 1 legend.** Stacked horizontal bar of Gaia launch mass (n = 1 spacecraft; total 2030 kg as reported by the ESA Gaia factsheet; both masses assumed rounded to the nearest 10 kg). The propellant segment (400 kg, **19.7 %** of total, filled) occupies the left of the bar and the non-propellant remainder (1630 kg, **80.3 %**, hatched) the right; segment boundaries fall at 0 / 400 / 2030 kg. No error bar is drawn on the segment boundary because no measurement uncertainty is published; instead the source-rounding band on the propellant share (**19.4 – 20.0 %**, §5 S1) is annotated at the right of the bar as a bracketed range. Percentages are rounded to 1 d.p. and the segments sum to 100.0 %.

## 9. One-line audit statement

> Propellant mass was **19.7 %** of the 2030 kg launch mass (400 kg / 2030 kg; 1 d.p.; source: ESA Gaia factsheet — edition and access date to be recorded by the reviewer; source-rounding band 19.4–20.0 %).
Reversible factual lookup and arithmetic ratio for rough test-chamber comparison; no safety-critical or committed action.

quotes.whole:
[Updated from Julian Date 2451800.5 (13 September 2000) on 22 Dec 2021]
Semimajor axis (106 km)          Approximate mean distance from the Sun (or other central
body in the case of satellites) from center to center in
10^6 kilometers.
Sidereal orbit period (days)     The time it takes the body to make one revolution about
the Sun relative to the fixed stars in days.
For Pluto, it is the time from the last zero longitude
crossing to the next (24 July 1820 - 2 July 2068).
Tropical orbit period (days)     The average time for the body to make one revolution
about the Sun from one point in its seasonal orbit to
the equivalent point (e.g. equinox to equinox) in days.
For Earth, this equals exactly 1 year. Not known for Pluto.
Synodic period (days)            The time interval between similar configurations in the
orbit (e.g. opposition) of the body and Earth, in days.
Perihelion (106 km)              The point in a body's orbit closest to the
Sun, in 10^6 kilometers.
Aphelion (106 km)                The point in a body's orbit furthest from
the Sun, in 10^6 kilometers.
Mean orbital velocity (km/s)     The average speed of the body in elliptical orbit,
in kilometers/second.

verdict.summary:
Deliverable: NASA-fact-sheet pressure ratio (draft for qualified scientist review)

1. Source lock and date
- Earth: NASA NSSDCA Earth Fact Sheet, https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/earthfact.html, Last Updated 15 November 2024 (DRW). Retrieved copy timestamp 2026-11-23T12:05:54Z.
- Mars: NASA NSSDCA Mars Fact Sheet, https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/marsfact.html, Last Updated 19 May 2025 (DRW). Retrieved copy timestamp 2026-11-23T12:05:54Z.
- Date check for 2026-11-21: both page revision stamps precede 2026-11-21, and the retrieved copies carry those stamps. No revision between 21 and 23 November 2026 is indicated. An exact 2026-11-21 archival snapshot was not independently available in this run; this is a provenance caveat, not a value ambiguity.
- Units: mb = millibar = hPa = 100 Pa; 1 bar = 10^5 Pa (NASA fact-sheet notes).

2. Values used
- Earth surface pressure: 1014 mb (Earth Fact Sheet, Terrestrial Atmosphere, line 'Surface pressure: 1014 mb'). Use the listed value, not the standard atmosphere value of 1013.25 hPa.
- Mars surface pressure at mean radius: 6.36 mb (Mars Fact Sheet, Martian Atmosphere, line 'Surface pressure: 6.36 mb at mean radius (variable from 4.0 to 8.7 mb depending on season)'). Use 6.36 mb only; the seasonal range and the Viking 1 Lander site values are excluded per the instruction.

3. Calculation
P_E = 1014 mb = 101,400 Pa
P_M = 6.36 mb = 636 Pa
R = P_E / P_M = 1014 / 6.36 = 101400 / 636 = 159.433962264...
Rounded to one decimal place: 159.4
Check: 6.36 mb x 159.4 = 1013.784 mb, which is 0.216 mb below 1014 mb (0.02%).
Units: mb/mb cancels; R is dimensionless.

4. Uncertainty and sample size
- The fact sheets give no measurement uncertainty and no sample size; these are summary values, not measurements made in this laboratory. Sample size: N/A.
- Rounding-level envelope: Earth +/- 0.5 mb, Mars +/- 0.005 mb. Linear envelope gives 1013.5 / 6.365 = 159.23 and 1014.5 / 6.355 = 159.64; report 159.4 with an envelope of about +/- 0.2. Combining the two rounding terms in quadrature gives about +/- 0.15. The one-decimal result remains 159.4.
- Sensitivity, not used: Mars seasonal extremes 4.0 to 8.7 mb give 116.6 to 253.5; a Mars midpoint of 6.35 mb gives 159.7; Earth standard 1013.25 hPa with Mars 6.36 mb gives 159.3. These alternatives show why the specified mean-radius value and the listed Earth value matter.
- Precision note: the requested one-decimal format yields 159.4; the tenths digit is the first uncertain digit under the rounding envelope.

5. Reporting table
Quantity | Value | Unit | Uncertainty | Sample size
Earth surface pressure | 1014 | mb (hPa) | +/- 0.5 (rounding) | N/A
Mars surface pressure at mean radius | 6.36 | mb (hPa) | +/- 0.005 (rounding) | N/A
Earth/Mars pressure ratio | 159.4 | dimensionless | +/- 0.2 (rounding envelope) | N/A

6. Interpretation and review
Earth's listed surface pressure is about 159.4 times Mars's mean-radius surface pressure. For test-chamber set points this is a rough scaling only: Mars surface pressure varies seasonally from 4.0 to 8.7 mb and varies by site, so an actual Mars chamber set point should be chosen separately and reviewed by a qualified scientist before any chamber change. The ratio itself does not set a chamber pressure.

7. Reproducibility steps
1) Open the Earth Fact Sheet URL and read 'Surface pressure: 1014 mb'.
2) Open the Mars Fact Sheet URL and read 'Surface pressure: 6.36 mb at mean radius'; ignore the parenthetical seasonal range.
3) Compute 1014 / 6.36 and round half-up to one decimal place. No other transformations are applied.

verdict.summary:
Scope and provenance. This is a documentary correction, not an experiment; there is no sample size, and the only uncertainty is the precision stated in the errata (0.1 K). Primary record: NASA NTRS Document ID 19770009539, U.S. Standard Atmosphere, 1976, NASA-TM-X-74335 / NOAA-S/T-76-1562, published 1 October 1976. The NTRS PDF at https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19770009539/downloads/19770009539.pdf contains an appended 'Errata Sheet for 19770009539.pdf', an email from Yekta Gursel to NASA HQ-STI-INFODESK dated Thursday, 8 January 2015, 5:34 PM. The errata sheet's item 2, under 'Table 2, B. Category II Constants, on Page 2', reads: '2) The value for Sutherland's constant S is too small by 0.4. It should be 110.4 Kelvin.' The surrounding text identifies this as an error in Table 2, B. Category II Constants of the document. This is the operative NTRS-distributed errata text used here. I did not find a separately signed NASA correction memo; the correction is the errata sheet included in the NTRS PDF.

Original published value. The document's Table 2, B. Category II Constants, gives S = 110 K (Hilsenrath et al. 1955, as cited in the standard). The DTIC/Internet Archive text of the same document independently shows: 'The Sutherland constant, S = 110 K, (Hilsenrath et al. 1955) is a constant in the empirical expression for dynamic viscosity.'

Arithmetic. Corrected S = 110.4 K. Published S = 110 K. Difference = 110.4 K - 110 K = 0.4 K. The document's value was therefore too small by 0.4 K (one decimal place, the precision stated in the errata). The errata's '0.4' is unitless in the sentence but takes the unit of S from the following '110.4 Kelvin'; hence 0.4 K, not 0.4%.

Answer to the code question. If the code uses the USSA 1976 dynamic-viscosity form mu = beta T^(3/2)/(T + S) with T in kelvin and beta = 1.458e-6 kg/(s m K^(1/2)), enter S = 110.4 K. This is the constant alone in the denominator, not the sum (S+T). If the code's temperature variable is in degrees Rankine, convert consistently: S = 110.4 K x 1.8 deg R/K = 198.72 deg R, and use T in deg R. Do not mix K and deg R. If the code uses a different Sutherland reference-temperature form, the same physical correction is 0.4 K in the temperature-like constant; verify the formula before substituting.

Sanity check and impact. The corrected value 110.4 K is the commonly used Sutherland constant for air, so the errata is physically plausible; this is a sanity check only, and the authority is the errata. At 288.15 K, replacing S = 110 K with 110.4 K changes mu by the factor (288.15 + 110)/(288.15 + 110.4) = 398.15/398.55 = 0.998996, i.e. corrected mu is about 0.100% lower at that temperature. This is a derived illustration, not a measured value; it uses the stated formula and temperatures.

Result entries. Ask 2: 110.4 K. Ask 3: 0.4 K.

References. verdict.summary:
# Corrected turbulent thermal conductivity k_t — U.S. Standard Atmosphere 1976, Table III, 0 m

Draft for review by a qualified scientist before use in any heat-transfer calculation or publication.

## 1. Answers

| Ask | Quantity | Value | Unit |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Corrected k_t, as printed units | 2.5362 × 10⁻² (0.025362) | J/(m·s·K) |
| 2 | Same quantity, SI heat-transfer units | 0.025362 | W/(m·K) |

Both entries are the same physical quantity; the numeric value is unchanged by the unit change (Section 4).

## 2. Traceability of inputs

- **Original value.** U.S. Standard Atmosphere, 1976 (NOAA/NASA/USAF), Table III, entry at 0 m geometric altitude: k_t = 2.5362 × 10⁻⁵ J/(m·s·K). Five significant figures as printed.
- **Correction.** NASA erratum to USSA-1976, stating that this Table III entry is too small by a factor of 1000 (factor as quoted in the request). Taken as an exact scale factor of 1.000 × 10³.
- **Documentary caveat for the reviewer.** The erratum document number, revision date, and the exact column/row scope of the correction were *not* independently opened in preparing this draft; the factor is applied as stated in the request. The reviewer must attach the precise erratum citation (document identifier, date, affected table and column) before this number is published or used in a design calculation.

## 3. Correction arithmetic

k_t(corrected) = 2.5362 × 10⁻⁵ J/(m·s·K) × 1.000 × 10³
               = 2.5362 × 10⁻² J/(m·s·K)
               = 0.025362 J/(m·s·K)

This is a pure three-place decimal shift. No rounding is introduced by the correction itself: the five printed significant figures (2, 5, 3, 6, 2) are carried through unchanged. Direction check: "too small by a factor of 1000" means the true value is larger, so the printed value is multiplied (not divided) by 1000; dividing would give 2.5362 × 10⁻⁸, which is physically impossible for a gas (Section 6).

## 4. Unit conversion J/(m·s·K) → W/(m·K), verified dimensionally

- J/(m·s·K) = (N·m)/(m·s·K) = N/(s·K) = (kg·m·s⁻²)/(s·K) = kg·m·s⁻³·K⁻¹
- W/(m·K) = (J·s⁻¹)/(m·K) = (kg·m²·s⁻²·s⁻¹)/(m·K) = kg·m·s⁻³·K⁻¹

Both reduce to kg·m·s⁻³·K⁻¹, so 1 J/(m·s·K) ≡ 1 W/(m·K) exactly (the definition 1 W = 1 J/s is exact in SI). Conversion factor = 1.000 (exact), therefore:

k_t = 2.5362 × 10⁻² J/(m·s·K) = 2.5362 × 10⁻² W/(m·K) = 0.025362 W/(m·K).

## 5. Significant figures and uncertainty

- **Significant figures:** 5 (2.5362), preserved through the correction.
- **Rounding half-width (source print only):** the last printed digit of 2.5362 × 10⁻⁵ sits in the 10⁻⁹ place; the half-unit rounding bound is 5 × 10⁻¹⁰, which becomes 5 × 10⁻⁷ after multiplying by 10³.
- **Reported as:** k_t = 0.025362 ± 0.0000005 W/(m·K) = 0.025362 ± 0.0000005 J/(m·s·K) (rounding half-width only; relative half-width 2.0 × 10⁻⁵, i.e. 0.0020 %).
- **What this is not:** no measurement uncertainty is stated for this entry in the source table, and the erratum factor carries no stated uncertainty (treated as exact). The ±5 × 10⁻⁷ above is a print-rounding bound, not a physical uncertainty. Any physical uncertainty must be quoted from the source's own statement, which is not reproduced in this draft.

## 6. Independent plausibility checks (all three must pass; they do)

**(a) Comparison with tabulated dry-air conductivity.** Standard reference tables for dry air at 1 atm give k ≈ 0.0223 W/(m·K) at 250 K and k ≈ 0.0263 W/(m·K) at 300 K (Incropera & DeWitt, *Fundamentals of Heat and Mass Transfer*, Table A.4 — values to be verified against the physical table by the reviewer). Linear interpolation to the sea-level standard-atmosphere temperature of 288.15 K:

k(288.15 K) ≈ 0.0223 + (38.15/50)(0.0263 − 0.0223) = 0.0223 + 0.003052 = 0.02535 W/(m·K).

Agreement with the corrected value: |0.025362 − 0.025352| = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ W/(m·K), i.e. 0.039 % — well inside the rounding and interpolation error of the cross-check (the two table entries carry ~±0.0001 W/(m·K) each). This is a plausibility check, not a validation.

**(b) Prandtl-number check.** With interpolated dry-air properties at ~288 K, μ ≈ 1.79 × 10⁻⁵ Pa·s and c_p ≈ 1.006 × 10³ J/(kg·K) (same source, same interpolation caveat):

Pr = μ c_p / k = (1.79 × 10⁻⁵ × 1.006 × 10³) / 0.025362 = (1.80 × 10⁻²) / 0.025362 ≈ 0.709.

Pr ≈ 0.71 is the expected value for diatomic air (kinetic theory gives Pr ≈ 0.7 for such gases). With the *uncorrected* value, Pr would be ≈ 709 — a factor 1000 too high and physically absurd for a gas. This is the decisive independent argument that the printed entry cannot be used as-is.

**(c) Order-of-magnitude check.** The uncorrected 2.5362 × 10⁻⁵ W/(m·K) is lower than typical aerogel insulation (~0.013–0.02 W/(m·K)) by three orders of magnitude; no gas at 1 atm has a thermal conductivity that low. The corrected value sits in the normal gas range. The corrected value 0.025362 W/(m·K) lies inside the 0.024–0.026 W/(m·K) band expected for air at sea level.

## 7. Reproduction recipe (deterministic; anyone can re-run by hand)

1. Open USSA-1976, Table III; read the 0 m geometric-altitude entry for k_t: 2.5362 × 10⁻⁵ J/(m·s·K).
2. Read the NASA erratum for Table III; confirm the stated factor is 1000 and that the direction is "value too small" (i.e. multiply).
3. Multiply: 2.5362 × 10⁻⁵ × 10³ = 2.5362 × 10⁻² J/(m·s·K).
4. Confirm the dimensional identity of Section 4 (1 J/(m·s·K) = 1 W/(m·K)), so no numerical factor is applied in conversion.
5. Record k_t = 0.025362 W/(m·K) with five significant figures and rounding half-width ±5 × 10⁻⁷ W/(m·K).
6. Run the three checks in Section 6; all must pass before the number is used.

## 8. Use in the sea-level heat-transfer calculation

The corrected coefficient enters Fourier's law as q″ = −k_t ∇T. For illustration only, a 10 K/m near-surface gradient gives q″ = 0.025362 × 10 = 0.25362 W/m² (per unit area, 1-D, steady, constant k_t). If the calculation uses a turbulent conductivity rather than the molecular value, confirm with the source which of the two Table III represents; the erratum-corrected number above is the molecular-scale thermal conductivity of air at 0 m.

## 9. Reviewer checklist and limits

- Attach the exact erratum citation (document number, date, affected table/column) — required before publication.
- Confirm the erratum applies to the whole k_t column, not only the 0 m row. If so, every other altitude entry in that column needs the same ×1000; this draft corrects only the 0 m entry as requested.
- Geometric vs geopotential altitude is moot at 0 m: H = z·r₀/(r₀ + z) = 0 when z = 0, so both conventions give the same entry.
- Verify the literature values quoted in Section 6 against the physical tables before citing them in a publication; they are used here only as order-of-magnitude checks.
- The stated ±5 × 10⁻⁷ is a print-rounding bound, not a measurement uncertainty; do not present it as an uncertainty budget for the atmosphere model.
- Status: draft. Not to be used in a design, safety, or publication context until a qualified scientist has confirmed the erratum citation and the checks in Section 6.

Key takeaways
The Bethe-Bloch formula gives the mean energy a fast charged particle loses per unit path in matter. The Particle Data Group (PDG) calls it the Bethe equation and says it holds for βγ from about 0.1 to 1000, with an accuracy of a few percent.
Stopping power falls roughly as 1/β² at low speed, reaches a broad minimum near βγ of 3 to 3.5 and then creeps upward in the relativistic rise.
A minimum-ionising particle in silicon loses 1.664 MeV cm²/g, which is 3.876 MeV/cm. A 300 µm layer takes a mean of about 116 keV.
The most probable loss in that layer is lower, about 84 keV, because a few rare hard collisions drag the mean up. That is why detector designers quote the most probable value.
Below βγ of roughly 0.1 the formula needs shell, Barkas and Bloch corrections. Electrons and positrons need a separate treatment.

Above βγ of about 1000 radiative losses start to matter, and the stopping power is no longer a function of βγ alone (PDG, section 34.2.3).
Below βγ of about 0.1 the projectile speed approaches that of atomic electrons. Adding shell, Barkas and Bloch terms keeps the treatment accurate to about 1 percent down to β of 0.05, which is about 1 MeV for protons.
Between β of 0.01 and 0.05 the PDG says there is no satisfactory theory, and fitted formulae are used. Below about 0.01 the Lindhard description of electronic stopping takes over.

quotes.whole:
Where the formula stops working
Above βγ of about 1000 radiative losses start to matter, and the stopping power is no longer a function of βγ alone (PDG, section 34.2.3).
Below βγ of about 0.1 the projectile speed approaches that of atomic electrons. Adding shell, Barkas and Bloch terms keeps the treatment accurate to about 1 percent down to β of 0.05, which is about 1 MeV for protons.
Between β of 0.01 and 0.05 the PDG says there is no satisfactory theory, and fitted formulae are used. Below about 0.01 the Lindhard description of electronic stopping takes over.
Heavy ions need extra terms for higher-order coupling and finite target size. These can change the loss by a factor of two or more for the heaviest nuclei.
Electrons and positrons are a separate case. The PDG gives them their own section, because the incoming electron is identical to the target electron in Møller scattering and the maximum energy transfer differs.
Thin absorbers raise a further issue. A few collisions cannot average out, so the real distribution is asymmetric and a single event can stray far from the mean. That is the subject of the Landau and straggling pieces linked above.

verdict.summary:
VERIFICATION NOTE — 2024 PDG passage-of-particles review, Eq. (34.5)

1. Source and version
Primary source: S. Navas et al. (Particle Data Group), Review of Particle Physics (2024), Phys. Rev. D 110, 030001 (2024), Sec. 34.2.3, Eq. (34.5), in the review 'Passage of Particles Through Matter', PDF rpp2024-rev-passage-particles-matter.pdf. The fetched copy at https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-passage-particles-matter.pdf carries the revision stamp '25th March, 2025'. A second fetched rendering at https://pdg.lbl.gov/2026/download/rpp-2025/reviews/rpp2024-rev-passage-particles-matter.pdf carries the stamp '31st May, 2024'. Both contain the identical validity sentence quoted below, so the version ambiguity between these two renderings does not affect the answer.

2. Verbatim statement in the review
Immediately following Eq. (34.5), the review states:

'Eq. (34.5) is valid in the region 0.1 . βγ . 1000 with an accuracy of a few percent. At βγ ∼ 0.1 the projectile speed is comparable to atomic electron “speed,” and at βγ ∼ 1000 radiative effects begin to be important (Sec. 34.6). Both limits are Z dependent.'

The dots in the fetched text are OCR renderings of the inequality signs; the statement is read as 0.1 ≲ βγ ≲ 1000. The phrase 'a few percent' is the review's own wording, not an analyst's paraphrase.

3. Answer to ask 1 — verdict
No. The stated validity region does not support applying Eq. (34.5) at βγ = 0.01 and claiming the review's few-percent accuracy. The lower bound of the stated region is βγ = 0.1. The requested point βγ = 0.01 lies a factor of 10 below that bound. The review attaches its few-percent accuracy qualifier only to the interval 0.1 ≲ βγ ≲ 1000; it states no exception, extension, or separate accuracy claim at βγ = 0.01.

4. Answer to ask 2 — stated βγ region
The βγ region over which the review states Eq. (34.5) to be valid with an accuracy of a few percent is:

0.1 ≲ βγ ≲ 1000, with βγ dimensionless (βγ = p/Mc).

5. Qualifications stated by the review
The review explicitly says 'Both limits are Z dependent.' It does not quantify that Z dependence, does not give a material-by-material table of the bounds, and does not state any condition under which the lower bound moves down to 0.01. It also identifies the two physical reasons for the limits: at βγ ∼ 0.1 the projectile speed is comparable to atomic-electron speeds, and at βγ ∼ 1000 radiative effects become important. The review's Section 34.2.3 is written for 'moderately relativistic charged heavy particles'; electrons and positrons are treated separately elsewhere in the review. Nothing in the quoted passage supports a species-, charge-, or material-specific exception that would extend the few-percent claim to βγ = 0.01.

6. Units, uncertainty, and sample size
βγ is dimensionless. The review quotes the bounds as 0.1 and 1000 with no numerical uncertainty and describes the accuracy only qualitatively as 'a few percent'; no standard uncertainty, confidence interval, or error band is attached to either the bounds or the accuracy phrase. Sample size is not applicable: this is a textual verification of a single statement in a review, not a measurement or a statistical estimate. The only 'uncertainty' relevant to this note is bibliographic (which rendering of the 2024 review is cited); the sentence is identical in both fetched renderings, so the verdict and interval are stable against that choice.

7. Bottom line for the detector analyst
The use at βγ = 0.01 is outside the review's stated validity region by a factor of 10 in βγ. The analyst may cite the review for the interval 0.1 ≲ βγ ≲ 1000 with a few-percent accuracy, subject to the review's Z-dependent caveat at the limits, but may not cite the review for a few-percent accuracy claim at βγ = 0.01.
